p01.why: const_cast can remove volatile from the target of a pointer.

p02.why: A volatile return type is deprecated, the compilers warn by default, and -Werror makes the warning an error.

p03.why: Accesses through a pointer to volatile to an object that is not volatile are valid, and a plain read of the same object is valid too, so main returns 0.

p04.why: A volatile member function can be called on an object that is not volatile.

p05.why: The implicit copy constructor takes const S&, which does not bind to a volatile object.

p06.why: The variable keeps volatile in its type, and the result of arithmetic on its value is a plain int.

p07.why: Writing one volatile bit-field reads and writes its unit, and the other bit-fields keep their values, so main returns 0.

p08.why: A volatile scalar can be read and copied into an int, which is 4, so main returns 0.

p09.why: Constant evaluation reads a volatile object.

p10.why: Member functions overload on volatile, so a.f() is 1 and b.f() is 2, and main returns 0.

p11.why: ++ on a volatile object is deprecated, -Wall warns, and -Werror makes it an error.

p12.why: A reference that is not volatile does not bind to a volatile object.

p13.why: The program reads a volatile object through a glvalue that is not volatile.

p14.why: The value of an assignment to a volatile object is used in a larger expression, which warns under -Wall, and -Werror makes it an error.

p15.why: read is not volatile, so it cannot be called on a volatile object.

p16.why: An ordinary constructor initializes the volatile object and sets v to 3, so main returns 0.

p17.why: The class declares a copy constructor that takes a const volatile reference, so the copy works and main returns 0.

p18.why: An implicit conversion cannot remove volatile from the target of a pointer.

p19.why: count = count + 1 is a plain read and write, not deprecated, and count reaches 5, so main returns 0.

p20.why: Every initializer gives its value, the zero-initialized variable is 0, and local returns 14, so main returns 0.

p21.why: Constant evaluation reads a volatile object through an int*; Clang rejects, GCC and EDG accept and the program returns 0 (Q-0320).

p22.why: Compound assignment and a plain assignment of v + 1 are not deprecated, so -Wall gives no warning.

p23.why: The parameter and return types are pointers to volatile, and the pointers themselves are not volatile, so no deprecation warning applies.

p24.why: 3, then 5, then 13; compound assignment is valid, so main returns 0.

p25.why: The implicit copy assignment is not volatile, so it cannot be called on the volatile object d.

p26.why: A volatile parameter type is deprecated, the compilers warn, and -Werror makes it an error.

p27.why: A conversion can add volatile to the target of a reference.

p28.why: An in-class initializer for a static const volatile int member; GCC and EDG accept, Clang rejects (Q-0080).

p29.why: A const volatile reference does not bind to a temporary.

p30.why: A const volatile variable at namespace scope has external linkage, so both units see one object and main returns 0.

p31.why: A structured binding declaration with volatile is deprecated, -Wall warns, and -Werror makes it an error.

p32.why: A constructor must not be declared volatile.

p33.why: A member of a volatile object is volatile, so its address converts to volatile int*.

p34.why: Overload resolution picks int& for a and volatile int& for b, so main returns 0.

p35.why: A destructor must not be declared volatile.

p36.why: The volatile member function is called on a volatile object and reads 2, so main returns 0.

p37.why: Conversions add volatile and then const to the target of the pointer.
